scopes.tasksWriteDetail: Append-only: it can add, never replace what someone wrote. Also builds the tree — spaces, folders and lists — so a new project can be set up in one go, and attaches files to a task (a screenshot, a log, a PDF).
scopes.tasksManageDetail: Move them between columns, and overwrite title, description or priority. Also corrects or withdraws comments you wrote — never anyone else's. Needed to mark work as done.
scopes.notesWriteDetail: Append-only: adds a new page, never touches one that already exists. What a migration from another notes app needs.
scopes.notesManageDetail: Overwrites a page's title or body outright — the note's own conflict/history safeguards still apply, but the content changes.
scopes.reportsWriteDetail: Append-only: add a comment or attach an image to a report.
scopes.reportsManageDetail: Change status, assignee, priority, category or area, remove a report's screenshots, and correct or withdraw comments <1>you</1> wrote — never anyone else's, which cac refuses outright.
scopes.collectionsWriteDetail: Leaves a described API ready to run. Creating only — editing, deleting and sharing one stay out of reach, sharing because it reaches other people.
scopes.docsWriteDetail: Append-only: adds to the end of a section and records decisions, and can never delete what somebody else wrote. Safe while a person has the document open.
scopes.docsManageDetail: Replaces a whole section and decides who a document belongs to. A save that arrives after somebody else's is refused rather than applied, but this is still the permission that can overwrite work. It cannot mark a document reviewed — that says a person confirmed it, and only a superadmin signs it.
scopes.deploysManageDetail: Set up how a service deploys — repo, branch, server builds, Dockerfile and its secrets <1>by name</1> — and register new ones. <1>Never</1> deploys, rolls back, deletes or changes the migration command; no secret value goes through it.
scopes.notifyMeDetail: Let an agent working with this token notify <1>you</1> — “I stopped: there is a decision to make” — in the bell, on your phone and as a desktop notice. Only ever you: there is no way to send it to anyone else.

ci.lead: The CI tells cac when it publishes a commit's image. On «Record», the CI keeps deploying as it does today and cac just keeps the list of versions.
ci.toDeployTitle: Have cac deploy every CI notice?
ci.toDeployBody: From now on, every commit the CI notifies about will be deployed on {{server}}. Remove the workflow steps that deploy over ssh, or it will deploy twice.
ci.noKey: No key: the CI doesn't notify yet.
ci.remintBody: The current one ({{preview}}) stops working right away: a CI using it will fail until you give it the new one.
ci.keyOnce: Save it now as the repo's CAC_DEPLOY_KEY secret: it won't be shown again.
ci.stepLead: Then add this step to the workflow, after the image is published. The sha has to be the one the image is tagged with.
ci.noBuilds: The CI hasn't notified about any yet.
ci.githubLead: With the GitHub App installed: each deploy shows up in GitHub, and when that workflow finishes well it counts as the CI notice, no curl step needed.

secrets.title: Secrets on the server (1Password)
secrets.lead: Where each of the service's secrets comes from. Rotating reads them on this machine and takes them to the server as Docker secrets: the container sees them at /run/secrets/NAME. Only the names reach cac.
secrets.notRegistered: This service isn't deployed from cac yet: register it in Services → Deploy to manage its secrets here.
secrets.empty: No secrets yet. Add one, or import them from a 1Password item.
secrets.name: Name
secrets.invalid: Each name in UPPER_SNAKE_CASE, no repeats, and each reference op://vault/item/field.
secrets.needsDeploy: Only a service that cac deploys can be rotated («Deploy» mode in its deploy): a CI's stack deploy would silently drop these secrets.
secrets.rotateBody: They're read from 1Password on this machine ({{names}}) and taken to {{server}}; the service restarts with them. Only the names reach cac.
secrets.rotated: Secrets rotated; the service restarted with them
secrets.unchanged: Already up to date: nothing restarted
secrets.bridgeTitle: The Dockerfile block that turns these secrets into environment variables
secrets.bridgeLead: Secrets arrive as files in /run/secrets. This entrypoint exports each one as a variable unless the environment already has it, and `exec "$@"` lets the same image run the app or the migrations job.
secrets.readArgs: Read build args from the Dockerfile
secrets.argsMerged: {{count}} build args in the Dockerfile: {{added}} added, {{promoted}} now used by both. Fill in the missing 1Password references and save.
secrets.captureSummary: First time: save what the service already runs in 1Password
secrets.captureLead: Reads the environment variables the CI left on the service and creates a new 1Password item with one hidden field per variable, named exactly like it. Values go from the server to 1Password: they never reach cac or the screen.
secrets.captureBody: Reads the environment of {{service}} on {{server}} over ssh and creates {{item}} with each variable as a hidden field. Nothing changes on the server.
secrets.captured: {{count}} variables saved in {{item}}. Review which the build uses, then save.
secrets.problemName: {{name}}: the name has to be CAPITALS_WITH_UNDERSCORES, up to 40
secrets.problemRef: {{name}}: its reference is empty or isn't op://vault/item/field
secrets.progressUpload: Taking them to the server and restarting {{service}}…
secrets.envNotMounted: “{{env}}” isn't mounted on this machine: without its .env it can't be checked or rotated.
secrets.rotateCommandLead: Optional. If the server has its own command to change the secrets (it reads KEY=value on stdin, like rotate-secrets), cac hands them to it instead of setting them its own way. With it you can rotate even when the CI deploys.

backups.title: Backups
backups.lead: Databases on this server that cac backs up. The agent makes each backup inside the database's container, encrypts it for the keys below and uploads it to a bucket where it cannot be deleted before its time. Downloads stay encrypted.
backups.empty: No database is backed up from cac yet.
backups.disabled: Backups are not configured on this cac (no bucket). Nothing can be scheduled.
backups.agentOld: This server's agent is v{{version}}; backups need v{{min}}. Update the agent from the overview.
backups.recipientsLead: Backups are encrypted for these public age keys. Only whoever holds the matching private key can open them — it is not stored in cac.
backups.keyInvalid: That is not an age public key (age1…). Never paste the private one.
backups.keyHelp: Generate one with age-keygen -o backups.key, keep the whole file in your password manager, delete it from disk, and paste only the line that starts with age1.
backups.removeKeyBody: New backups will no longer be encrypted for it. Existing ones still open with it.
backups.deleteBody: Its schedule is removed. Backups already taken stay in the bucket until their retention ends.
backups.downloadBody: You get the encrypted file for five minutes. It opens with: age -d -i backups.key file.age > backup
backups.credentialEnvHint: The name of the variable in the container that holds the credential. cac never sees its value.
backups.retained: In total, about {{n}} backups kept at a time.
backups.createLead: The desktop app generates a new age key in memory and saves it straight into 1Password: the private half never touches the disk or this page. Only the public half is added here.
backups.opUnavailable: 1Password is not reachable: install the op CLI, sign in, and turn on the desktop app integration.

engine.text: Which database runs in that service. It decides how the backup is made: SQL Server with BACKUP DATABASE, PostgreSQL with pg_dump.

service.text: The Swarm service the database runs in. The agent goes into its container to make the backup there.

database.text: The database's name inside the engine, not the service's. In SQL Server it is the one in the database explorer; in PostgreSQL, the one \l lists.

credentialEnv.text: The name of the container's environment variable that holds the credential. The agent uses it inside the container and cac never sees its value. In SQL Server it is the sa password; in PostgreSQL, the database user.

every.text: How many hours between backups. The options divide the day or are whole days, so it always lands at the same time.

at.text: The time of the first backup of the day; the next ones add the interval. Every 6 h from 03:30 runs at 03:30, 09:30, 15:30 and 21:30. Best in quiet hours.

timezone.text: The time zone of that time, in IANA format. The time holds across daylight-saving changes.

keepDays.text: Each backup is kept at least this many days and then deletes itself. With one backup a day, that is the last N days, one per day. Before that date nobody can delete it, not even with cac's keys.
keepDays.example: 7 = you can go back to any day of the last week

keepWeekly.text: On top of the dailies, the first backup of each week (Monday's) is not deleted after a few days: it stays this many weeks. It lets you go further back without keeping one for every day. 0 = no weeklies.
keepWeekly.example: 4 = you can go back to any week of the last month

keepMonthly.text: The same, by month: the first backup of each month (the 1st) stays this many months. It is what lets you go far back. 0 = no monthlies.
keepMonthly.example: 6 = you can go back to any month of the last half year

restoreEvery.text: Every how many days cac takes the latest backup, restores it into a temporary database, checks it has its tables and drops it. That is how you know the backups really work. 0 turns it off; not recommended.

enabled.text: Turned off, the database stops being backed up but keeps its settings and the backups it already has.

backups.databaseHint: The database's name inside SQL Server or PostgreSQL, not the service's.

summary.lead: You will be able to go back to:

backups.testBody: It restores a full copy of {{db}} on the same server and checks all of it. Meanwhile and for a few minutes after, the database can be slower for the website's users. The automatic test already runs at night; by hand, better outside busy hours.
